meta.description: The White Queen, in Chapter V of Through the Looking-Glass (1871). Verbatim — and she is boasting about practice, not whimsy.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Why, sometimes I've believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast'?
meta.ogDescription: Lewis Carroll wrote it; the White Queen says it, in Through the Looking-Glass. Not the Red Queen, not the Mad Hatter, and not Alice.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: Word for word from Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There (Macmillan, December 1871), Chapter V, “Wool and Water”. The White Queen says it, replying to Alice’s complaint that one can’t believe impossible things; Carroll wrote it.

source.heading: The passage

docMeta.dd: Through the Looking-Glass, and What Alice Found There
The White Queen, to Alice — both fictional characters

source.excerpt:
Alice laughed. “There’s no use trying,” she said: “one can’t believe impossible things.”

“I daresay you haven’t had much practice,” said the Queen. “When I was your age, I always did it for half-an-hour a day. Why, sometimes I’ve believed as many as six impossible things before breakfast.”
trail: Checked against the full text. The exchange appears verbatim in the complete Project Gutenberg edition of Through the Looking-Glass ↗, in Chapter V, “Wool and Water” — the chapter in which the White Queen turns into a sheep.

Independently confirmed on Wikiquote. The Through the Looking-Glass page ↗ transcribes the same passage under its Chapter 5 heading, attributing it to the White Queen, with wording identical to the Gutenberg text.
The first edition text is on Wikisource. The Wikisource text of Chapter V ↗ carries the book as published, for checking against the original Macmillan printing rather than a modern transcription.
source.excerptNote: Quoted alone, the line reads as a celebration of whimsy. In context it is a retort: the Queen is telling Alice that believing impossible things is a skill, and that Alice is simply out of practice.

author.name: Lewis Carroll
author.heading: About Lewis Carroll
author.bio: Lewis Carroll was the pen name of Charles Lutwidge Dodgson, a mathematics lecturer at Christ Church, Oxford. Under the pseudonym he wrote Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland (1865) and Through the Looking-Glass (1871); under his own name he published on geometry and logic. He was also a prolific letter-writer, and a good deal of what circulates as “Carroll” online comes from that correspondence rather than the Alice books.

misattribution.heading: What usually goes wrong
misattribution.intro: The wording survives intact. The speaker rarely does.

items.why: Swapped constantly, because Through the Looking-Glass has two queens and the Red Queen is the more famous. This is the White Queen, in Chapter V; the Red Queen is the chess-board drill-sergeant of Chapter II.
A frequent caption, but the Hatter belongs to the other book — Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland — and is not in this scene at all.

Also seen, and exactly backwards: in the book Alice is the one who says she can’t believe impossible things, and the boast is the Queen’s reply. The confusion has a clear source — in Tim Burton’s 2010 Alice in Wonderland it is Alice who counts off six impossible things ↗, steadying herself before she fights the Jabberwocky.

misattribution.truthLine: Carroll wrote it, the White Queen says it, and it sits in Chapter V of Through the Looking-Glass ↗.

context.heading: Believing as a discipline
lead: The joke is mathematical, which is unsurprising from a man who lectured on logic at Christ Church. The White Queen treats belief the way a tutor treats scales: something you drill daily, half an hour at a time, until you can manage six impossibilities before breakfast.

It has since been adopted almost universally as a motto for imagination and optimism — which is a perfectly good use of it, and the opposite of what the scene is doing. Carroll’s Queen is faintly ridiculous, and her expertise is in believing things that are not true.
